articles.title: “I was a Leash kid”: How Travis Kelce hilariously revealed his mom put him on a Leash as a child, and the reason behind it
articles.summary: Travis Kelce was the kind of toddler who could not stay put, and his mother Donna had a fix.
articles.body: Travis Kelce was the kind of toddler who could not stay put, and his mother Donna had a fix. Talking with his brother Jason on the New Heights podcast, the Chiefs tight end laughed about it. “I was a leash kid, yeah,” he said. The "leash" was really a safety harness. Travis started walking at eight months old and kept bolting. Donna used the harness for about six months, mostly at busy outings and festivals. She had a reason. Jason had once wandered off at a county fair, and a police officer had to bring him back.Why Travis Kelce was a leash kidThe story came up in an October episode of New Heights. Travis told it as a joke, but the setup was practical. He was walking at eight months old. Most babies take their first steps closer to a year, so Donna had a baby with a head start and no sense of where to stop.“She eventually got pissed and sick of us getting lost, and she put me in a … leash. I was a leash kid, yeah,” he said.The harness was her answer for crowded places. Picture a fairground on a summer weekend: noise, lines, food stands, and a baby who already knows how to run. Donna says she used it for about six months, and only on those busy outings. Nothing permanent.“You put it around your shoulders, you’d connect it twice,” he added before joking that he remembered, “just dragging my parents across the entire amusement park [yelling] ‘Let me go!’”Travis, of course, called it a leash. That word is funnier than harness, and it gave the podcast segment its hook. The early walking also fits the player he became. A tight end needs quick feet and a lot of motor. Travis was already moving before his first birthday.Jason's county fair scare behind the harnessThe reason came from the other Kelce. Earlier on, Jason had gotten lost at a county fair, and a police officer was the one who brought him back. That is the kind of afternoon a parent does not forget. When a second son turned out to be a runner, Donna was not going to hope for better luck.So the harness had a clear job. Big crowds, short window, no repeats. Donna explained the reasoning when the story came up, which tells you she saw it as a safety call and not a quirk.It helps to see how ordinary this is. Parents of runners have used child harnesses for a long time, and online opinions on them swing both ways. In a packed fairground, though, most parents are thinking about one thing, which is knowing where their kid is. Donna kept hers to a limited stretch and moved on.There is also a nice symmetry in the Kelce family story. One brother got lost and needed a police officer to find his way back. The other would not stop moving and needed a strap. Both grew up to host a podcast together.Not every parenting call becomes a podcast bit decades later. articles.title: Jonathan Taylor's Wife Ayanna Questions Colts Future in Trending Video After Buckner, Nelson Trades
articles.summary: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor is one of the biggest names to watch on the trade market, and his wife is tired of the uncertainty.
articles.body:
Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor is one of the biggest names to watch on the trade market, and his wife is tired of the uncertainty.

Ayanna Taylor took to social media to give her thoughts on the situation around the Colts after DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson were traded on Tuesday.

"Is literally anyone safe on this team? ... It feels like rookie year all over again. So naturally my mind is spiraling," she said. "What does this mean for my husband and I? Do I need to start packing our bags? Are we even going to be spending our daughter's first Halloween together? Will we make it to game day, or was last week the last time my husband is putting on a Colts jersey? ...What are we going to do without Quenton Nelson?"

The Colts have already fired general manager Chris Ballard, and at 2-5, they were clearly going to be sellers ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

The firesale began on Tuesday, with Indianapolis sending Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in return for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Later in the day, the Colts traded Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round draft pick.

Taylor could likely earn the Colts the biggest return of any other player. The star running back has rushed for 587 yards and an NFL-best eight touchdowns on 140 carries.

The question is whether Indianapolis is even interested in trading him. ESPN's Adam Schefter reported on Tuesday that the Colts prefer to move on from players like Josh Downs and Grover Stewart before Taylor.

"They don't want to trade Jonathan Taylor, which doesn't mean they won't trade him, but I don't think they want to, and today I would say they don't," Schefter said on the Pat McAfee Show . "But there are other players that I believe will wind up being on the move here. And I think the players you look at would be DeForest Buckner, Josh Downs, Grover Stewart on the defensive line."

The Colts' hesitancy to trade Taylor makes sense, considering they signed him to a new two-year, $44 million extension just two months ago.

But what the team wants to do and what makes the most sense might not be the same thing. If the Colts are focused on the future, trading Taylor might be the best move.

articles.title: How Patrick Mahomes has spent nearly $12 million on real estate across Texas and Missouri without ever buying a home in Los Angeles, Miami, or New York
articles.summary: Patrick Mahomes has earned more than most athletes ever will, yet his property map is small.
articles.body: Patrick Mahomes has earned more than most athletes ever will, yet his property map is small. Public reports show a Kansas City condo, a larger home nearby, eight acres in Belton, Missouri, and a mansion in Westlake, Texas. Together they point to a portfolio estimated near $12 million. No Los Angeles penthouse, no Miami waterfront, no Manhattan address appears in the records. The Chiefs quarterback signed a $503 million contract in 2020, and what he did with that security says plenty about how he plans to live.How Patrick Mahomes built a $12 million property portfolio in two statesThe $12 million figure needs context. Press reports describe four purchases: a $350,000 condo in December 2017, a $1.8 million house in January 2019, an eight-acre lot in Belton reportedly bought for about $400,000 in 2020, and a Westlake mansion at roughly $3.37 million. Those prices add up to about $5.9 million.A 2023 New York Post report, picked up by The Real Deal, put the portfolio near $8 million once current values and the Belton house were counted. Reaching $12 million means including construction costs and today's market estimates, and nobody has itemized those publicly. Treat it as an estimate, not a receipt.The pattern is easier to trust than the total. Every property sits in the two states that shaped him. Missouri is where he works. Texas is where he grew up.The $350,000 condo that started it allMahomes was a 22-year-old rookie when he closed on his first place in Kansas City. The condo covered about 1,800 square feet, with two bedrooms and three bathrooms. He paid $350,000 against a $475,000 ask, which suggests a young player who negotiated like someone who planned to be around a while.Plenty of first-round picks buy something flashy the moment a check clears. This was a modest, sensible home in the city that drafted him. It was a small bet on staying.The $1.8 million Kansas City upgradeBy January 2019, Mahomes was already the face of the franchise. He bought a 4,300-square-foot house on West 57th Street for $1.8 million. The Real Deal later reported its estimated value at about $2.2 million, a decent return for a house that served mainly as a stepping stone.Sports Illustrated reports he eventually sold a Kansas City home after moving into his custom compound. That fits the way he has handled property: buy well, upgrade when life changes, and don't hold what he no longer needs.Why Belton, Missouri, became the centerpieceThe Belton purchase is the most telling one. Mahomes signed his record extension in the summer of 2020, then bought a vacant eight-acre lot south of Kansas City. He could have bought any finished mansion on the market. He chose empty land.What he built there is unusual even by NFL standards. Reports describe a private football field, a par-3 golf hole, an indoor basketball court, a pool, and a pond. The compound serves as the family's primary residence during the season.The appeal is obvious for a quarterback with two young children and a famously large public profile. Eight acres buy privacy, and privacy is hard to find when you are the most recognizable person in a metro area. It also lets him practice, play, and relax without leaving the property.The Westlake mansion that keeps Texas closeMahomes was born in Tyler and played at Texas Tech, so a Texas base makes sense. Around the start of the pandemic, he bought an 8,000-square-foot mansion in Westlake, near Dallas, for about $3.37 million. The asking price was reportedly $4.26 million. The New York Post reported he bought it from the estate of former Chargers tackle Andrew Gissinger III.The house has four bedrooms, seven bathrooms, a wine room, and a kitchen with breakfast seating for 12. It overlooks the Vaquero golf course. Reports say he uses it as an offseason home, training there in the spring and summer.It is the most expensive home he owns, and it is the one tied most closely to family and roots rather than football. The two-state setup splits his year cleanly. Missouri is for the season. Texas is for everything else.Why Los Angeles, Miami, and New York never made the listPublic records show no purchases in the glamour markets, and the reason is worth thinking about instead of assuming. Mahomes is not a transplant chasing a lifestyle. He is a hometown-adjacent star who has tied his business life to Kansas City. He holds minority stakes in the Royals, Sporting Kansas City, and the KC Current, so his money and his reputation both stay local.Texas also has no state income tax, which helps an athlete spending half the year there. Still, tax rules rarely explain a person's choices alone. Players owe taxes in every state where they play games, so a coastal condo would not have solved a tax problem. It would have added a third address to manage.Most of all, the portfolio looks like it was built around where his people are. A third city would not fit that.What his approach says about athlete wealthThe common story about pro athletes and money is a rapid climb followed by overspending. Mahomes' real estate record reads differently. A below-ask condo, a profitable upgrade, a land play, and a discounted Texas mansion show patience at every step.Whether the total is $8 million or $12 million matters less than the discipline behind it. Four properties, two states, no trophy homes in famous zip codes. For a man with a $503 million contract, that is restraint.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Joey Porter Jr. Calls Out Critics After Cowboys' Win vs. Eagles, 'They'll Be Quiet Soon'
articles.summary: Certain NFL fans and pundits questioned if Dallas Cowboys' cornerback Joey Porter Jr. missed a Week 5 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers because he wasn't happy with the team not giving him a contract extension rather than the illness that was listed on the injury report.
articles.body:
Certain NFL fans and pundits questioned if Dallas Cowboys' cornerback Joey Porter Jr. missed a Week 5 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers because he wasn't happy with the team not giving him a contract extension rather than the illness that was listed on the injury report.

But Porter—who missed the first four games of the season while embroiled in a contract dispute with the Pittsburgh Steelers before being traded to Dallas—isn't bothered by the speculation.

"Me personally, I know the real," he told Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram . "I know the truth. I don't really pay too much attention online to what they have to say. I just got to keep doing my job on Sundays. Once they see the tape, they'll know. They'll be quiet soon."

The 26-year-old has appeared in three games for the Cowboys and has been quite good, only allowing one catch for five yards while being targeted nine times. Thus far, he's enjoyed his role in Christian Parker's defense.

"[He's] put me in a good position to really hone in on the defense and hone in on my task," he told Harris. "It's not too hard for me on the boundary when I just have to eliminate guys. That's exactly what he wants me to do, and I'm just going to keep doing that."

articles.title: Bo Nix's Broncos, Bane and Big Foot - Inside the Denver sporting empire luring fans 5,280ft in the clouds
articles.summary: Visit Denver hosted Sky Sports in Colorado to see what fans can expect from one of the biggest and most famous sporting hubs in the United States; watch the Denver Broncos host the Kansas City Chiefs, live on Sky Sports NFL from 9.25pm on Sunday
articles.body:
It would become a storied intimidation tactic that has since translated across to their current home Empower Field, but perhaps too an unwritten cheat code to thousands 'getting their steps in', given all I would come to learn of this fitness-enthused Mountain West metropolis.

Here was your proverbial protein shake of Colorado goodness, unbridled escapism and blood-pumping self-care flexing in the clouds some 5,280ft above sea level, as if detached from the rest of the nation. They breathe a little differently here, operate a little differently, attack sport a little differently.

The city is serene and soothing in accordance with its neighbouring nature, and yet its sporting disciples deafening. From its mountainous backdrop to its rich variety of wildlife, Denver is a laptop screensaver picture of tranquillity. From its sunrise joggers to its rock-scaling climbers, it is a breeding ground for adrenaline and activity. And between its seven major league sports teams, it is a cauldron of intense, ever-expanding fandom.

Welcome to Mile High, where an early awakening at the Limelight hotel (fuelled by some jet-lag) would kickstart my stay with a stunning sunrise view over Union Station, around which bustled coffee-grabbers, job-goers and worm-catching early birds.

For further information, head to visitdenver.com

I had flown in directly from London Heathrow for a dose of Denver life, another West Brom-come-Broncos fan I met that weekend had made the trip from Birmingham, and each week Sean Payton's side receive support from neighbouring states in New Mexico, Montana, Utah and Wyoming. Such is their isolated geographical position in the metaphorical 'Gods' of America, the Broncos reign supreme as a prized NFL attraction.

Saturday. My choice of cargo trousers in bronzeable heat had already come back to haunt me in a land where shorts and t-shirt tend to top the attire. Denver's 300-days of sunshine each year lend themselves to a city driven by life outside and an accompanying will to explore. This Brit stuck out, a reality only amplified by the perplexed look upon learning bars and clubs close earlier here in order to avoid squandering mornings better dedicated to fitness and training; party early, workout early. And for what it is worth, the motivation and zest to stay on the move becomes infectious.

By night, Red Rocks Amphitheatre is known as Denver's unique home of world-class music acts, where Lily Allen had been headlining on her album tour at the time of my visit. By morning, it appears to adopt the appearance of an outdoor gym, with its multiple tiers of theatre steps occupying yoga classes and workouts for families and friends of all ages.

One man is shadow boxing back-and-forth in a mask reminiscent of Batman villain Bane, a father and his four children are tackling the steep incline in unison from bottom to top and one elderly gentleman is performing kettle bell swings at the awe of younger workout partners. It is enough to guilt-trip this sluggish journalist after an evening of down-time watching the Colorado Rockies baseball team and exploring Denver's world class breweries; Ratio Beerworks, for curious travellers, and Whiskey Bar, where I witnessed the most competitive round robin of snooker games - they take sport and winning seriously here, no matter the game or level.

The Rockies these days are a little less associated with success in comparison to tavern snooker and their Broncos brothers, having reached the playoffs just five times since 1993. Still, they retain a devoted fanbase that preserve baseball's unique pass-time entertainment. On this occasion families were invited to a fireworks show, dare I say to compensate for the lack of Rockies fireworks on the field. And yet their supporters keep coming back.

The Broncos, as mentioned before, top the sporting charts in Denver as three-time Super Bowl champions and one of the most successful franchises in NFL history. The team boasts the longest active sell-out streak for an NFL franchise that has remained in one city, dating back to 1970, contributing to a 20-year wait-list for season tickets.

Denver initially played their football in Mile High Stadium from 1960 to 2000, before moving into Empower Field at Mile High in 2001. The organisation is now targeting the 2031 NFL season as a completion date for their new retractable roof stadium, which would account for the Colorado elements as well as offering year-round use of the facility for events beyond football. Recent history points towards an increased chance of hosting the Super Bowl for stadiums that have a roof or can be covered.

The Broncos are the only team in the NFL to announce the number of 'no-shows' on the big screen during each home game, prompting boos from fans in attendance towards those who didn't make the journey.

Right on cue, the jeers arrived late in their Week Two victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars, where I was among 76,472 fans basking in Colorado sunshine to soak up a day that began with the Broncos' traditional pre-game skydiving Thunderstorm show and ended in a first win of the season for Bo Nix's side.

It is raucous, rattling noise from start to finish, underlining one of the most renowned fan bases in football. Oh, and boy do they hate the Kansas City Chiefs, whose travelling fans shall be alerted to that fact - if not already aware - when they head to Mile High this weekend, live on Sky Sports NFL.

They cut the figure of overlords, empowered by their respiratory nuances high in the sky, reminding teams of where they are with an unmissable sign reading: "ELEV 5280′ Altitude Sickness is Real" as opposition players walk into the stadium.

It creates an 'us versus them' unity among Broncos fans, and yet it remains a city warm and welcoming to its visitors; I met one Cowboy hat-wearing local fascinated by a British accent, so too a stadium worker who had a friend living in Clapham - because OF COURSE. It's always Clapham.

Empower Field has also served as host for events ranging from Barack Obama's Democratic presidential nomination acceptance in 2008 to Taylor Swift concerts. In March 2026 it also made history by setting a new National Women's Soccer League attendance record when 63,004 fans watched the Denver Summit expansion team play the Washington Spirit, surpassing the previous benchmark of 40,091 set by Bay FC at Oracle Park.

Denver natives do not mess around when it comes to sport. If there is a team, a game, an individual for whom to root - they are there. There are enough of them; just three years ago the Nuggets won the NBA Finals, and four years ago the Colorado Avalanche won NHL's Stanley Cup.

The Summit are something of Denver's newest, thriving hope having been accepted as an NWSL expansion team in January 2025, with legendary Broncos quarterback Peyton Manning part of their ownership group. Six Summit players were recently called up to represent the US Women's National Team during the October international break. That included midfielder Lindsey Heaps, who has won a World Cup, two Olympic medals and captained her side at the 2023 World Cup across more than 170 caps for the national team.

I attended Summit's 2-1 win over Seattle Reign, where a sold-out crowd of 12,272 watched on despite an hour-long rain delay. Chants of 'you can't do that' at the sight of a foul was a unique Americanism contrary to the more profane tirades customary to European football, but it proved yet another crowd reflective of Denver's deep-rooted sporting devotion.

Beyond its sport it is a city embodied by its gateway to the natural world.

Dedicated Broncos fans might know 'Frank the Tank' as being the childhood nickname for offensive tackle Frank Crum, while others may know it to be the legendary moose bull of Rocky Mountain National Park. Sadly (or perhaps fortunately), a day trip into the mountains did not lead me to Frank.

What it did lead me to was the otherworldly sights of Mount Blue Sky, where never-ending greenery, the whisper-inciting Echo Lake, Idaho Springs and scenic road loops along which Walter Mitty might skateboard delivered lifelong images for the mental archives. So too a buoyant tour guide who would inform us of his potential Big Foot encounter while camping in the surrounding forest area; I saw his photos, and the foot-prints are almost believable enough to sway the most stubborn of naysayer.

Anyway, it is a perfect calming complement to the city's Broncos mania, where ziplining and whitewater rafting still preserves Denver's commitment to sporting adrenaline. The views are truly something else.

It is as versatile a sporting city as you might find in the United States, my deepest regret being my inability to ski such is the access to some of the world's greatest slopes.

Denver's RiNo district plays host to trendy shops, phenomenal street murals and the multiple cuisines of Denver Central Market. It is a community that offers a reminder to Denver's diversity, with Hispanic and Latino residents making up roughly 34 per cent of the city's population - and no doubt contributing to my faultless gameday chilaquiles at The Bindery.

Shopping in Cherry Creek, the Denver Art Museum, the city's eight Michelin-starred restaurants and easy access to the Rocky Mountains occupy some days, while sport on tap awaits on every other.

Bring your shorts, and a Broncos jersey.

For more information, visit visitdenver.com .

articles.title: Justin Jefferson's charity bowling night raised over $45,000 for cancer research; the Vikings star also surprised 7-year-old fan Claire Van Epps, who is undergoing treatment, with Super Bowl tickets
articles.summary: Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson has raised more than $45,000 for cancer research through a charity bowling event, while giving a young
articles.body: Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson has raised more than $45,000 for cancer research through a charity bowling event, while giving a young fan undergoing treatment an experience she is unlikely to forget. The NFL star and his JJets Foundation hosted the inaugural “Strike Out Cancer” fundraiser for the American Cancer Society (ACS), bringing together cancer patients, survivors, caregivers and Vikings teammates. According to announcements published by the Minnesota Vikings on October 6 and the NFL Players Association (NFLPA) on October 9, 2026, Jefferson also surprised seven-year-old Claire Van Epps, who has been undergoing treatment for Ewing sarcoma, with two tickets to Super Bowl LXI.The event raised funds for cancer research and support services while giving 25 cancer patients, survivors and caregivers an opportunity to meet Jefferson and spend time with the football star. The evening included bowling, games and a silent auction featuring sports memorabilia, including signed helmets, game-worn cleats and a Randy Moss jersey.Jefferson was joined by his older brother, Jordan, and Vikings teammates Aaron Jones Sr., Andrew DePaola and Johnny Hekker. The gathering also marked an important step for the JJets Foundation, whose work Jefferson described as a family effort shaped by personal experiences with cancer.Seven-year-old fan receives Super Bowl surpriseAmong the guests was Claire Van Epps, a young Vikings supporter whose cancer journey has been marked by remission and relapse. According to the team's report, Claire was diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma in 2023. She initially entered remission but experienced a relapse shortly before Christmas in 2025. Claire is currently undergoing oral chemotherapy. Despite the challenges of treatment, the Vikings described her as a cheerful child who loves watching the team and was thrilled to meet her favourite player in person.Jefferson spent time talking with Claire, encouraging her and posing for photographs. The wide receiver said he had seen pictures of the young fan wearing his jersey while undergoing cancer treatment and found it inspiring that she looked up to him. The evening became even more memorable when Claire's family won a football autographed by Jefferson through a raffle. The player then called her to the front of the room and presented her with oversized tickets to Super Bowl LXI, scheduled for February 2027.The surprise prompted cheers from the crowd, while Claire and her parents reacted with excitement. The tickets offered the young fan an opportunity to watch one of American football's biggest events alongside her family. The gesture was part of a wider effort to connect with people whose lives have been affected by cancer. For Jefferson, the event was an opportunity to listen to their experiences, recognise their challenges and use his public profile to draw attention to the disease.More than $45,000 raised for cancer researchThe NFLPA named Jefferson its Week 5 Community MVP on October 9 in recognition of the fundraiser and his broader charitable work. The organisation confirmed that the bowling event raised more than $45,000 for the American Cancer Society to support cancer research. The ACS works to advance cancer research, improve patient outcomes, advocate for people affected by the disease and help patients access care. Angie Rolle, the organisation's senior vice-president for partner engagement, told the Vikings that money raised through the event would support research breakthroughs, improved treatments and efforts to make care more affordable. Jefferson has also taken on the role of an American Cancer Society ambassador, helping raise awareness about cancer and the experiences of patients and survivors.The fundraiser included a silent auction featuring an LSU helmet, a Vikings helmet and Jefferson's signed game-worn cleats. A signed Randy Moss jersey was among the other items available to bidders. The NFLPA also announced a $10,000 donation to the JJets Foundation following Jefferson's selection as Community MVP. The award recognises NFL players who make significant contributions to their communities away from the field.A wider commitment to community workSince joining the Vikings in 2020, Jefferson has supported several community initiatives in Minnesota and his home state of Louisiana. According to the NFLPA, the JJets Foundation has reached more than 1,500 children through programmes that include youth football camps, school laptop donations and holiday initiatives.Jefferson has also supported young cancer patients. In September 2026, he surprised two children from Children's Minnesota, Ada and Arthur, with personalised shoes inspired by his own Crucial Catch cleats. Ada had been treated for Wilms cancer and was declared in remission in July 2024, while Arthur had been diagnosed with B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma and experienced substantial vision loss during treatment.The shoes were customised to reflect the children's experiences, including Arthur's name written in Braille. Jefferson also spent time with them at the Vikings' training facility, where they received team merchandise and watched practice.The initiatives coincide with the NFL's Crucial Catch campaign, which promotes cancer awareness and encourages early detection. Jefferson's role as an ACS ambassador has added another dimension to his community outreach, allowing him to connect with families dealing with the disease.For Claire and her family, the bowling night offered a moment of celebration amid an ongoing medical journey. For the JJets Foundation, the fundraiser marked the beginning of an initiative aimed at raising money, supporting patients and creating opportunities for families affected by cancer.The event's $45,000-plus contribution will support the American Cancer Society's work, while Jefferson's Super Bowl ticket surprise gave one young fan something special to look forward to as she continues treatment.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: NFL: Why did Jalen Hurts play for the Philadelphia Eagles with a blood clot?
articles.summary: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is recovering from a life-threatening condition which developed after he was cleared to play with a blood clot and board a long-haul flight.
articles.body:
News that Jalen Hurts played a game hours after being diagnosed with a blood clot had already shocked the NFL world.

The Philadelphia Eagles then said their star quarterback will probably miss the rest of the season after multiple blood clots were found in his lungs - a life-threatening condition if not treated quickly.

It raised questions over the NFL's handling of the matter and its general approach to player health and safety, partly because the game in question was part of the league's international series.

Hurts' initial diagnosis was in London, before the Eagles played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on 11 October, and he flew back with the team that evening.

What do we know about what happened? Why was Hurts allowed to play and then fly home straight after? And what does it mean for him, the Eagles and the NFL?

Sunday, 4 October: Another player stepped on Hurts' left calf during Philadelphia's defeat by the Los Angeles Rams, although he completed the game.

Thursday, 8 October: Hurts first reported an issue to the team. He trained in full all week and had treatment on Thursday and Friday.

Saturday, 10 October: The Eagles arrived in London in the morning and Hurts visited the Cleveland Clinic that evening. An ultrasound showed he had a superficial blood clot (vein thrombosis) in his calf but he was cleared to play on Sunday.

Sunday, 11 October: Hurts returned to the team hotel at about 3am before playing the full game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. A follow-up ultrasound was recommended within 72 hours and Hurts was cleared for the flight home.

Wednesday, 14 October: After receiving daily treatment, Hurts had another ultrasound, which showed the clot had moved, and he was ruled out of the next game.

Monday, 19 October: Joint statement by the Eagles and Hurts' agent said further tests showed he now has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli (multiple blood clots in both lungs).

His treatment will involve blood-thinning medicine and he should make a full recovery but is expected to miss the rest of the season.

Some of the initial reports said that Hurts did not sleep for 36 hours before playing in London, but his agent later confirmed that he slept after returning to the hotel and also at the stadium.

Dr Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, was in London that weekend and arranged for Hurts to be evaluated at the Cleveland Clinic, an American-owned private hospital which is an official supplier of sports medicine services for the NFL's London games.

The NFL has protocols in place for concussions, emergency preparedness and extreme heat, for games in the US and overseas.

But, speaking at a news conference last Tuesday, Sills explained the league does not have a protocol for situations such as this.

Nevertheless, Sills said that those who dealt with Hurts were "incredibly conservative" and that he had "complete confidence" in how the Eagles handled the situation.

Later that day, the NFL Players Association (NFLPA) called for a full investigation, adding that the NFL "previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care [Hurts] received".

However, on Sunday the league and NFLPA released a joint statement saying they are "working together to review the matter".

'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on

The NFL's next international game is in Madrid on 8 November and the local medical co-ordinator is Real Madrid's chief medical officer, Dr Niko Mihic.

Dr Mihic told BBC Sport that blood clots among athletes are "not that common" and remembers in a previous role it took three visits for a baseball player to be diagnosed with a blood clot, because it is not something immediately associated with sports injuries.

Medical advice on whether to sleep and/or stay active is decided case by case. The same goes for whether it is safe to board a long-haul flight with a blood clot, as Hurts was allowed to do.

"It's not as simple as some people think," said Dr Mihic. "There's an amount of judgement that goes into this. It's like you're stuck between a rock and a hard place, but then you make your call."

As he and the NFL finalise their medical preparations for the Madrid game, Dr Mihic expects them to discuss scenarios such as that involving Hurts.

Asked what the NFL can learn from Hurts ultimately getting blood clots in his lungs, the league's Dr Sills replied: "I don't think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process.

"Sometimes in medicine we do all the right things and other things develop... but we have a committee that looks at all these cases."

What the NFL learned from Hamlin & Tagovailoa injuries

Whatever the outcome of the NFL's joint review with the NFLPA, the league will face greater scrutiny over how they handle players around games played overseas.

Players had a 16-hour flight for Australia's first NFL game in September, while the NFLPA's executive director JC Tretter expressed safety concerns over the quality of the field for the game in Brazil.

There are a record nine international games this year and, although the NFL ultimately wants 16 per season, Tretter added that "the goal has to be growing the game while maintaining the standards our players deserve".

Only Hurts knows how he feels about the way he was treated by his team and the NFL's doctors, but even before this issue there had been talk of the 2025 Super Bowl MVP leaving the Eagles.

Even if he does make a full recovery and returns to action, the 28-year-old will always have to bear blood clots in mind.

"The worst risk factor for recurrent embolisms is having had one previously," said Dr Mihic.

As for Philadelphia, they do not have an experienced quarterback in reserve and back-up Tanner McKee could not prevent them suffering a fifth straight defeat on Monday.

They were beaten 38-21 at home by the Dallas Cowboys to extend their longest losing streak under coach Nick Sirianni, so this could be a long season for the injury-hit Eagles.

Or with the trade deadline two weeks away, this could be the start of a rebuild for a team that reached two of the past four Super Bowls.

articles.title: Why Richard Sherman believes 49ers’ DeForest Buckner trade was an ‘absolute steal’
articles.summary: DeForest Buckner is returning to the San Francisco 49ers after the Indianapolis Colts traded the veteran defensive tackle in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round...
articles.body:
DeForest Buckner is returning to the San Francisco 49ers after the Indianapolis Colts traded the veteran defensive tackle in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round draft pick. Not only is 49ers tight end George Kittle excited about Buckner's arrival , but former NFL star Richard Sherman also praised the move, describing it as a steal for San Francisco.

During an episode of his "Richard Sherman Podcast," Sherman expressed his excitement about Buckner's addition.

"49ers are bringing the boys back home. Brought back Debo Samuel, brought back Dre Greenlaw, and now bring back DeForest Buckner," Sherman said. 'Eric Armstead, you better be looking at your phone because that's what kind of year it seems like for the San Francisco 49ers .

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"I think that's an incredible addition, a big time addition to a guy that's gonna make a great difference on this team. And they got him for only a 2027 fourth round pick. That's a steal."

Buckner began his NFL career in San Francisco after the 49ers selected him with the seventh overall pick in the 2016 NFL Draft. He spent four seasons with the franchise before being traded to the Colts in March 2020 in exchange for a first-round draft pick.

Buckner's return should provide an immediate boost to San Francisco's interior defensive line. He started all seven games for Indianapolis this season, recording 31 tackles and four sacks while continuing to demonstrate his ability to pressure opposing quarterbacks.

Across his seven seasons with the Colts, Buckner recorded 47 sacks, 122 quarterback hits and six forced fumbles. He also earned first-team AP All-Pro honors in 2020 and was selected to the Pro Bowl twice.

Buckner's experience and familiarity with the 49ers could also help him adjust to the defensive system quickly. With San Francisco holding a 6-1 record and competing for the NFC West title, the veteran defensive tackle gives the team another established presence.

The 49ers are now set to take on the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.

articles.title: ‘Get Your Facts Straight’ — NFL Fans Rip Dan Orlovsky For Failing To Grasp Why Bears Didn’t Go All-In on DeForest Buckner Trade
articles.summary: The Indianapolis Colts have shaken up their roster ahead of the NFL trade deadline, sending DeForest Buckner back to the San Francisco 49ers for a 2027 fourt...
articles.body:
The Indianapolis Colts have shaken up their roster ahead of the NFL trade deadline, sending DeForest Buckner back to the San Francisco 49ers for a 2027 fourth-round pick. The move came shortly after Indianapolis traded Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks, signaling a major shift toward building for the future.

ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky, however, had questions about why the Chicago Bears didn't do more to land Buckner. His take didn't sit well with fans, who pushed back by pointing out that the veteran defensive tackle wanted to return to San Francisco.

NFL Fans Push Back Against Dan Orlovsky's DeForest Buckner Take

During an appearance on ESPN, Orlovsky questioned why the Bears passed up the chance to acquire an established defensive tackle for a fourth-round pick.

"And then honestly, one of my big takeaways is how does Chicago not make this move? For a fourth-round pick," Orlovsky said .

At first glance, the price looked reasonable for an established interior defender. Buckner is in the final year of his contract, and his ability to pressure opposing quarterbacks could have strengthened a Chicago defensive unit that ranks 18th in PFN's Defense Impact Score with a 74.8 grade.

But fans argued that the draft compensation was only part of the equation. Reports indicated that the Bears had interest in Buckner, but the 32-year-old reportedly preferred to return to San Francisco, the team that selected him with the No. 7 overall pick in the 2016 NFL Draft.

One fan directly called out Orlovsky, writing, "@danorlovsky7 are you really so dense to not realize Buckner wanted back in SF and colts honored that?"

Another wrote , "Percent boy is unaware Buckner preferred 49ers (former team)."

A third fan added , "He wanted to be on SF. Please report this correctly."

Others were equally blunt about the situation. "Let me explain it like you're a child. He didn't want to come to Chicago. He wanted to go back to the team that drafted him and that was SF," one user wrote .

Another fan summed up the criticism by pointing to two key details: "2 things. 1. The bears did attempt to trade for Buckner. 2. He wanted to go to San Francisco. Get your facts straight."

PREDICT THE NFL SEASON: PFN's Free NFL Playoff Predictor

For the 6-1 49ers, bringing Buckner back would help address several injuries on their defensive line. Alfred Collins (patellar tendon) and C.J. West (knee) have been sidelined, while star edge rusher Nick Bosa has also missed time dealing with a calf injury.

The veteran has recorded 31 tackles and four sacks through his first seven games of the 2026 season. Buckner also ranks fifth in PFN's Defensive Tackle Impact Score with a 91.2 grade.

San Francisco is coming off a 29-20 loss to the Atlanta Falcons. After a Week 8 bye, the 49ers will look to bounce back when they face the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.

articles.title: Steelers miss out on Colts All-Pro trade sweepstakes
articles.summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers missed out on a huge trade for one of the best offensive linemen in the entire NFL.
articles.body:
It's official: The Pittsburgh Steelers , like the rest of the NFL, lost out on the trade sweepstakes for an All-Pro offensive lineman from the Indianapolis Colts .

On Tuesday, the Colts made shockwaves by sending arguably the best guard in all of football, Quenton Nelson, to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for near pennies on the dollar. In all, the Colts received 2027 third- and 2028 fifth-round draft picks from the Seahawks in exchange for Nelson. Considering the Steelers ' need to upgrade one of their guard positions and their ability to exceed this trade price with two 2027 third-round picks at their disposal, this could've been a home run for Pittsburgh.

Nelson, who was drafted by the Colts in the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft, was considered by many to be one of the best guards of his generation, making 129 starts and earning three First-Team All-Pro selections, three Second-Team All-Pro selections, and eight Pro Bowl honors during his first eight years in the league.

Although the Steelers missed out on Nelson, the team is still expected to pull off a "semi-big" move for a wide receiver as the trade deadline nears.

articles.title: Former Seahawks' 3rd-round pick would make sense for Commanders
articles.summary: The Commanders should look to add a former Seahawks' third-round pick after Seattle traded for Quenton Nelson.
articles.body:
There was a big trade on Tuesday. Actually, there were two, as the Indianapolis Colts shipped a pair of former first-round picks to the NFC West. The Colts sent eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks for two draft picks. Later, Indianapolis traded three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner back to the San Francisco 49ers, where he played his first four NFL seasons.

While adding veterans, especially those on expiring contracts, to a 1-4-1 team doesn't make much sense for the Commanders , Nelson could still have helped. The 30-year-old Nelson remains the NFL's top guard, and he's missed just four games in his nine-year career. Nelson also plays left guard, which is a question mark for Washington. Could you imagine an offensive line with Nelson and Cosmi at guard, and Laremy Tunsil (when healthy) at left tackle? It's a nice thought, but it was never a reality. Nelson wanted to land with a contender and may not have signed an extension.

But Nelson's trade did lead to another interesting transaction. After acquiring Nelson, the Seahawks released a 2024 third-round pick: guard Christian Haynes. The 6-foot-3, 317-pound Haynes played collegiately at Connecticut before going No. 81 overall in 2024. Haynes is a native of nearby Bowie, Maryland. Could Washington be a potential landing spot for Haynes?

Haynes appeared in 16 games as a rookie, but did not start. Last season, he began the year on injured reserve before returning to play in eight games. Haynes appeared in seven games for Seattle this season, including five starts at right guard for the injured Anthony Bradford.

Here's NFL.com's Lance Zierlein's draft profile on Haynes in 2024:

Four-year starter and team captain who is sturdy at the point of attack. Haynes plays with football intelligence and sees every snap as a mandate to move opponents and finish blocks. His draft slotting could be affected by a lack of length and being limited to one position, but his determined playing style counters those factors. He's not overly rangy but wipes out targets on pulling blocks and is capable in space, and in pass protection. The hand usage can get sloppy, allowing opponents to slip away from him, and he has a tendency to do too much grabbing. All things considered, he might outplay his draft slotting and become a solid NFL starter.

While Haynes' NFL career may not have started the way he wanted, he's only 26. If you're a team like the Commanders with offensive line issues, Haynes would be a smart waiver claim. What could it hurt? And even if Washington claims Haynes and he doesn't develop into a starter, he's quality depth for the rest of this season and next.

articles.title: Who will be ESPN 'College GameDay' guest picker for IU football game vs Minnesota? Names to know
articles.summary: The fourth-ranked Indiana Hoosiers host Minnesota, and IU will have ESPN's "College GameDay" on campus. Who do you want to see as celebrity guest picker?
articles.body:
For the second time in three years, ESPN's traveling pregame show is paying a visit to Bloomington.

ESPN announced Sunday that "College GameDay" would be held in advance of No. 5 Indiana football hosting Minnesota . In a rather weak slate of games, and despite a big SEC rivalry game, there is plenty at stake as the Hoosiers (7-1, 4-1 Big Ten) host P.J. Fleck 's physical Golden Gophers (5-2, 3-1). There is still a path to the Big Ten championship game and College Football Playoff for each team.

The previous visit to IU came outside Memorial Stadium, an opportunity to blend the gameday atmosphere with GameDay. But it was also before the reintroduction of a mascot, Hoosier the Bison, who was created for moment's like this : when former IU coach Lee Corso would pick a mascot's headgear and wear it to cap the show. And while IU didn't have the headgear then, it did recreate an iconic bus moment for Corso as part of a reunion with his 1979 Holiday Bowl team .

IU announced the set will be on campus at Showalter Fountain , which should give fans plenty of time for it to wrap up around noon and get over to Memorial Stadium for the 3:30 p.m. game. Who will be the guest picker alongside Rece Davis, Desmond Howard, Nick Saban, Kirk Herbstreit and Pat McAfee? Here's a look at a number of potential guests with IU ties (listed alphabetically).

You may not even have known, but Clayton Anderson had his song " Indiana " played on TV broadcasts during the Indiana football run to the national championship. The native of Bedford is a proud IU fan and has opened a bar in downtown Indianapolis with a Nashville-style sign .

From deadpan reactions to helping lead the New York Knicks to a NBA championship , OG Anunoby has plenty of reasons to be celebrated. How about this champion celebrating with the reigning football champions on his former campus? It'll be a tough time crunch, though. The Knicks play in Philadelphia on Friday night, but not again till Monday.

For the sake of promotion, Caitlin Clark makes the list. And her locale of greater Indianapolis as Indiana Fever superstar fits. And while Clark and Nike would surely love a chance to promote her Caitlin 1's again, that just happened Oct. 3 for "College GameDay's" visit to Ohio State at Iowa, which was the fourth most-watched show at 2.9 million per ESPN PR . Surely the Hawkeyes grad who also said she supports Notre Dame won't be the guest picker, not at an adidas school. Or will the ratings dictate otherwise?

WNBA superstar Caitlin Clark from Dowling Catholic to Iowa Hawkeyes to Indiana Fever

Some would say Corso riding into retirement wearing Brutus the Buckeye's head was perfect. How about one more time with Hoosier the Bison, which was created specifically for brand recognition like this? I mean, come on.

Businessman, entrepreneur and former "Shark Tank" star Mark Cuban has been around IU football. He's a known supporter of fellow Pittsburgh native Curt Cignetti , and has proudly supported the program financially .

It certainly feels like Tyrese Haliburton is becoming Indiana's biggest supporter, the state that is. Could the superfan and Pacers star return from a late tip-off Friday night in Miami for 'GameDay' before the Pacers return to action Sunday evening? Would an unashamed Iowa State fan and Wisconsin native be welcome for that opportunity?

Before he made a name for himself as Jason Jordan in WWE, Nathan Everhart was a three-time NCAA championship qualifier for the Hoosiers wrestling team. He was 38-3 in his senior year and ranked No. 2 nationally, finishing with 89 career victories and runner-up in the Big Ten in 2010.

Tried and true, John "Cougar" Mellencamp has had "Hurt So Good" play across Memorial Stadium and other stadiums, and the IU alum also played during the national championship celebration in January. Seems like an easy pick.

The world is a different place, private jets and all, but it would be difficult for Fernando Mendoza to make a pit stop in Bloomington ahead of the Las Vegas Raiders' game against the New York Jets. Similarly, his star receiver Omar Cooper Jr. would seem unlikely.

Fernando Mendoza of Indiana football plays for Las Vegas Raiders in NFL preseason debut

Which leads us to younger brother Max Mendoza, who wants to be a media personality and already aired on ESPN windows during the NFL preseason, the "Pat McAfee Show" at the ESPY's and more. IU fans and the country fell in love with the Mendoza family story, so if the Heisman-winning quarterback can't make it, why not have his brother realize a dream?

Have you seen "Glee," or the news that there is a reboot coming ? The initial series, written by one-time IU journalism major Ryan Murphy, aired on Fox but the reboot is going to Disney+ and Hulu, which are sisters to ESPN.

The five-time IndyCar champion could be his sport's greatest of all-time, and the native Spaniard has made Indianapolis home and fallen in love with American sports. That is largely because of IU football, and he has made several appearances on Fox's "Big Noon Kickoff" and drove out the Indy car against Ohio State.

Behind the scenes of Alex Palou and Hoosier the Bison's promo video

Screenwriter and film producer Angelo Pizzo was instrumental in popular sports films "Hoosiers" and "Rudy." A 1971 IU grad, Pizzo is coming up on the 40th anniversary of "Hoosiers," a fitting opportunity for extra promotion around the film and celebration, even if it is a basketball film on a football pregame show.

A former IU quarterback who had a nine-year NFL career as a receiver won a Super Bowl in 2005 with the Pittsburgh Steelers. He's the wide receivers coach/assistant head coach with the Chicago Bears, though, who play Monday night in Seattle. So not an impossible opportunity.

How do you top Kyle Schwarber wearing an IU batting helmet? How about Jasper native Scott Rolen, who frequents the Bloomington area. The Baseball Hall of Fame selection was a seven-time All-Star, eight-time Gold Glove winner and won the 2006 World Series with the St. Louis Cardinals.

Yes, Sage Steele is one of IU's trustees. She also left ESPN after settling a free-speech and retaliation lawsuit against ESPN and parent company Disney.
